name: Vancomycin
high_alert_note: Not confirmed as high-alert on a source read; the institution's list governs.
summary: Antibacterial used for serious infections caused by susceptible organisms such as methicillin-resistant staphylococci. Nursing priorities include serious infusion reactions versus anaphylaxis, renal injury, hearing symptoms, blood-count concerns and clinician/pharmacy-led exposure monitoring.
evidence_type_note: The evidence here is a regulator product label (prescribing information written for prescribers and pharmacists). It is not a bedside nursing practice guideline: the nursing actions are inferences from label warnings, marked partial, and the unit's protocol governs practice. A targeted check on 2026-11-21 additionally read the 2020 ASHP/IDSA/PIDS/SIDP executive consensus summary for serious invasive MRSA; that guideline supports AUC-guided exposure management in its defined population and does not supply a nursing dosing protocol.
jurisdiction_note: US FDA label only. EMA, MHRA and SFDA labels were not read; indications, warnings and presentations differ by country and by manufacturer.

FDA infusion pump page (high-risk infusion examples)

items.text: The label indicates vancomycin for treatment of serious or severe infections caused by susceptible strains of methicillin-resistant staphylococci and other listed organisms.
Give only as the pharmacy's preparation and the order direct, and stop the infusion and report any infusion reaction.

Verify the infusion-product form, secure IV access, prescribed pharmacy preparation, local infusion process and the requested blood-sampling timing. In patients with changing renal function or co-administered nephrotoxic drugs, prompt pharmacy/prescriber reassessment rather than adjusting the regimen independently.
Monitoring frequency and alarm limits follow the unit's protocol for this medicine.

The label warns rapid administration may cause exaggerated hypotension, including shock and rarely cardiac arrest, so the infusion should run slowly rather than as a rapid bolus; it also calls for monitoring renal function in all patients, especially those with renal impairment or who are also receiving a nephrotoxic drug, since systemic exposure increases the risk of acute kidney injury. The label describes ototoxicity (which may be transient or permanent) as more common with excessive doses, pre-existing hearing loss, or a concomitant ototoxic drug, and lists severe skin reactions and Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhoea among its warnings.

For serious invasive MRSA infection, the 2020 ASHP/IDSA/PIDS/SIDP monitoring consensus prefers individualized AUC-guided therapeutic drug monitoring rather than relying only on the older high-trough strategy. This specific recommendation is not automatically generalizable to other infections. The pharmacist/prescriber chooses sampling times, exposure targets and dose adjustments; bedside nurses verify timely sampling and report delayed/missed concentrations per local protocol.

In addition to renal function, monitor and report new hearing changes or tinnitus, and review blood-count results when treatment is prolonged or the patient also receives drugs associated with neutropenia (specific manufacturer's October 2026 US label).

Rapid bolus administration may be associated with exaggerated hypotension, including shock and rarely cardiac arrest; the label says infusion reactions usually stop promptly when the infusion is stopped.

Systemic vancomycin exposure may result in acute kidney injury, and the risk increases as serum levels rise; the label advises monitoring renal function in all patients, especially those with renal impairment.
Infusion-related events can occur during or soon after rapid infusion.

Rapid-infusion flushing, pruritus and hypotension may reflect a vancomycin infusion reaction, but severe airway symptoms, wheeze, breathlessness, hypotension or generalized urticaria may indicate anaphylaxis or another life-threatening emergency. Stop or pause the infusion according to emergency policy, immediately assess airway/breathing/circulation and activate emergency response when indicated; do not assume that a serious reaction will resolve simply because the infusion has stopped.

The October 2026 US label reports potentially permanent hearing toxicity, especially with pre-existing hearing loss, reduced renal clearance or other ototoxic drugs; severe skin reactions, extravasation/tissue injury, antibiotic-associated diarrhoea and reduced neutrophil counts are further hazards to recognise and escalate.

Infusion reactions include pruritus, erythema/flushing, urticaria, chest or back discomfort, and hypotension; the label also reports anaphylaxis. Respiratory symptoms or circulatory instability require emergency assessment rather than assuming a transient infusion response.

Serious renal toxicity, sometimes interstitial nephritis, can occur; risk increases with higher exposure, pre-existing renal dysfunction and other nephrotoxic medications. Hearing loss, tinnitus and vertigo have also been reported, with important long-term risks in susceptible patients.

The label describes reversible neutropenia and less common platelet or other blood-count changes, particularly relevant during prolonged courses; severe skin reactions, phlebitis and tissue injury after extravasation are additional recognized hazards.

Antibiotic-associated diarrhoea, including C. difficile-related disease, can occur during or after treatment. Clinical assessment and tests are directed by the treating team rather than automatically attributing all diarrhoea to the infusion.

At the first sign of a suspected serious infusion reaction, follow local emergency instructions for stopping/pausing the infusion, promptly assess airway, breathing, circulation and vital signs and notify the treating team. Activate emergency response for airway compromise, wheezing/dyspnoea, shock or suspected anaphylaxis; do not wait for symptoms to disappear. Also escalate reduced urine output/rising creatinine, new hearing symptoms, mucosal blistering, severe diarrhoea, or unexpected falling white-cell counts.

Use the unit's early warning score (for example, the Royal College of Physicians' NEWS2 track-and-trigger system) to standardise recognition of acute deterioration: a medium aggregate score is a key trigger for an urgent clinical review, and a high aggregate score triggers an emergency clinical response. This is a generic nursing escalation framework, not specific to this medicine; it does not replace this medicine's own escalation triggers, which remain local protocol.
Record the product and order checks, monitoring results, adverse events and escalation per unit standard.
Institution-specific preparation: follow your pharmacy's preparation standard and the product labelling. This library gives no preparation or concentration instructions.
Institution-specific dosing: follow the prescriber's order and your institution's approved protocol. This library gives no dosing instructions.

monitoring.text: Watch for flushing, rash and hypotension during the infusion.
Review renal function and drug levels as ordered.
Stop the infusion and report an infusion reaction at once.
Assess for wheeze, breathlessness, generalized urticaria and hypotension as possible anaphylaxis, not merely a routine rate-related infusion reaction; activate emergency response per local pathway.
Check ordered vancomycin sampling times and communicate with pharmacy; for serious invasive MRSA, the guideline favours AUC-based therapeutic monitoring instead of trough concentration alone.
Ask about hearing change or tinnitus and inspect the IV site for phlebitis or extravasation injury.
Review ordered complete blood count/white-cell trends during extended therapy or when combined with other marrow-suppressing medicines.

gaps: Vancomycin pharmacokinetic exposure/target selection, dose changes and exact level-sampling schedules remain the prescriber/pharmacist's responsibility; no dose or infusion-rate instructions are provided.
2020 AUC-guided monitoring recommendation is for serious invasive MRSA disease, and extrapolation to mild or non-MRSA infection needs independent expert review.
Renal replacement therapy, CRRT, obesity, pediatrics and unstable renal function require tailored local pharmacy/infectious-disease protocols not summarized here.
Specific infusion preparation, device instructions, secure IV access procedure and formal anaphylaxis protocol remain local.
Only the cited US Glenmark October 2026 vancomycin product and 2020 US-led consensus were verified; other manufacturers and EMA/MHRA/SFDA labels and any newer regional guidance remain unreviewed.
